I'm happy to share that my team won 1st place at Hack the Town hackathon sponsored by Google Play , presented by Hack the Hood ! We won $1800 :) and what's more exciting is to see my first app published on the Google Play Store! This was a 2-day event and my first hackathon experience. We built TrashGO, a community-driven platform designed to make neighborhood cleanups more accessible, engaging, and rewarding. Our goal with TrashGO was to create a platform where anyone can report local trash, discover cleanup events, and organize meetups to work together to clean up their communities. A big inspiration behind TrashGO was Pokémon GO. We wanted to take this idea of people meeting together and catching Pokemon and apply it to cleaning up neighborhoods. We plan to build upon this with gamified points and a rewards system that encourages users to participate, stay active, and be engaged. We also want to collaborate with local restaurants and businesses to offer benefits for members. In just two days, we built the full user experience, including authentication, an interactive map, event pages, progress tracking, event creation, scheduling, location finder, personal activity tracking, and an impact dashboard! Since this was my first hackathon, I learned so much about building under a tight deadline, turning an idea into a working product, designing around user needs, and collaborating with an amazing team. The most important lesson I learnt is building a good product isn't just about writing code or coming up with a solution, rather finding a real problem that solves a need while contributing to a meaningful cause and it's broader impact. A huge thank you to our awesome coach, Zain Shafique , for guiding us throughout the hackathon, helping us work through the idea, and pushing us to build TrashGO. I'm incredibly grateful to have built this with my team Owen Cruz, Solomon, Jason, and Johann. This was an amazing first hackathon experience, and I can't wait to continue my adventure of ideating and building! Check out our GitHub and Presentation: https://lnkd.in/gqNjTcnN https://lnkd.in/gtDucJVR

Just completed Non-Trivial 's 8-week Research Fellowship! 8 weeks ago, I set out to answer why gynecologic cancer screening rates are so low in LMICs, and instead, I ended up delving into whether cow dung can power a rural health clinic. I researched whether biogas could actually keep the lights on. Since then, I've written a full research paper and prototyped a web feasibility calculator on modular anaerobic digestion for Primary Health Centres in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, both biogas alone and paired with solar. Lots of pivots to get here, lots of numbers I had to walk back and redo, and one very memorable realization that the "exciting" variable wasn’t quite as impactful as I’d hoped it to be, but that’s the fun of researching and learning! I’ll finally present both my research and demo my tool this Wednesday, the culmination of 8 weeks of work. Once again, a big thank you to my facilitator, Vick Volovnyk , for helping me through it all and editing my paper even when it was a jumble of my thoughts; Jonah Boucher🔸 for setting up an amazing program; and the rest of the Non-Trivial community! You can find registration information here if you’re interested: https://lnkd.in/g5_scx-n #NonTrivialFellowship #RuralHealth #EnergyAccess #ClimateChange

So much to hold onto from Camp Abundance in Washington, DC earlier this month! The event brought together 100 students and recent grads to reconsider what people need from the government and how to get more of it. I was fortunate to give a talk, “Raging Against the Wrong Machine,” on how we can modernize government service delivery with AI. The technology we need exists, but we’re restrained by procurement cycles and a culture that embraces slow processes. Loved learning from public service leaders like Lynn Overmann and Giselle Hale, and a huge thank you to Victoria Ren and Maxwell Stern of Abundance Corps for putting this all together. Excited for what's ahead!

This summer, I learned the difference between a Windsor, a Four-in-Hand, and a Pratt knot. Eight weeks on Capitol Hill working for Congressman Ro Khanna 's office in Washington, DC taught me a lot of things. Learning to survive a DC summer in a full suit and tie was just the beginning. My first task was to tackle constituent mail. Every morning, I logged in to the office computer and faced an inbox filled with 50 to 500 messages concerning upcoming bills, personal grievances, and recommendations for the congressman. I didn't spend all day staring at the computer, however. Giving Capitol tours sharpened the communication skills I'd lean on for the rest of the internship. It laid the groundwork for meetings with Silicon Valley startups, NGOs, and organizations seeking bill co-sponsorship and a spotlight from one of the most tech-forward, progressive voices in Congress. The internship gave me real exposure to policy work: writing memos, bill recommendations for legislative aides, and researching future legislation. Digging into existing legislative frameworks (and finding where they could go further) reminded me what it actually takes to make change for people. I also wrote floor speeches for the congressman. Turning breaking news into short, sharp bullet points for his speeches taught me how much rhetorical weight a well chosen phrase can carry. None of it would've meant much without the team behind it. They spent hours teaching me the ins and outs of the NDAA, how bill development works internally, and how the congressman's ideas become real action. Thank you to the other intern and the office staff for an amazing summer. I hope to be back on the Hill next year!

I'm happy to share that Aditya Das , Zhiyu Wen , and I won 1st place in the Social Impact track at JacHacks SF! We built SafeRelay, an app that gets an emergency message out when there is no signal. When a natural disaster takes out cell towers, the people who need help most are the ones who suddenly cannot reach anyone, and responders end up working off incomplete reports. Mobile phones with satellite connectivity solve that for the few people carrying one, but not for a neighborhood full of ordinary phones. SafeRelay turns those phones into a peer-to-peer network. You write a distress packet in the field app and it hops phone to phone over Bluetooth, with every device storing it and passing it along. The first phone that gets any connectivity uploads the whole chain to the cloud, where an operations console shows what came in next to live USGS and NWS hazard feeds. Additionally, the Jachammer-powerd web console receives any packets sent by the mobile app, so that first-responders can easily view and prioritize off-grid emergencies. At this hackathon we wrote both the field app and the operations console in Jac, so the packet format, the relay rules and the server all lived in one language instead of three separate stacks. Capacitor handled the mobile shell and CoreBluetooth handled the iOS radio bridge, which is the part you can only really test on physical phones. Special thanks to Jason Mars, Vatsal Shah , Lingjia Tang and the rest of the JacHacks team for running it, and Jaseci Labs for Jac itself.
